## 1. Primary published triangle-free penny edge bound and missing bridge

Eppstein's theorem 4 states the edge count of **every** n-vertex triangle-free penny contact graph is at most

`2n - (1/2)*sqrt(2*pi*sqrt(3)*n+O(1)) = 2n - c0*sqrt(n)+O(1)`,

where `c0=sqrt(pi*sqrt(3)/2)=1.6494541661869015...`. Unit-separated point contact graphs are penny graphs after uniform scaling, and disconnected graphs are included. Thus a future proof that **every original unrestricted exact global minimizer** obeys `e >= 2n-(c0-epsilon)*sqrt(n)-C` for some fixed `epsilon>0`, `C` and all large n would prove Erdős #99 affirmatively. **No such lower bound was proved here.** Even a sharp triangle-free upper bound cannot alone force a triangle.

## 2. An all-global convex-hull shape estimate, not contact rigidity

Let `D_n` be the global minimum diameter and `H=conv X` for any original exact global X. Oler's `n <= (2/sqrt(3))*area(H)+perimeter(H)/2+1`, planar area <=`pi D_n^2/4`, and perimeter <=`pi D_n` yield

`sqrt(3/4+(2*sqrt(3)/pi)*(n-1))-sqrt(3)/2 <= D_n`.

The unit triangular lattice Voronoi covering radius `1/sqrt(3)` produces the independent upper bound

`D_n <= sqrt(2*sqrt(3)/pi)*sqrt(n)+2/sqrt(3)`.

The isoperimetric inequality `area(H)<=P(H)^2/(4*pi)` and Oler then give

`P(H)>=-pi*sqrt(3)/2 + sqrt(2*pi*sqrt(3)*(n-1)+3*pi^2/4)`.

Combining with `P(H)<=pi D_n` shows `0<=pi D_n-P(H)<=C(n)` with explicit

`C(n)=pi*(sqrt(2*sqrt(3)/pi)*sqrt(n)+2/sqrt(3))+pi*sqrt(3)/2-sqrt(2*pi*sqrt(3)*(n-1)+3*pi^2/4)`,

whose limit is `7*pi/(2*sqrt(3)) = 6.348297774820...`. This **shape-only** bound holds for every original global optimizer but supplies no original exact contact count. Source for Oler: https://doi.org/10.4153/CMB-1961-018-7 ; for lattice covering and this combination, credit **native Ramanujan + root rederivation**, not Oler as author of the combined formula. Keep `X,R,U,D` above with `diam(U)<D`, and choose removed `r in R` having **no unit contacts with any u in U**. ## Independent finite `n=4` classification

As detailed by original `w100_943`, in any four-point unit-separated set of diameter at most `sqrt(2)`, each angle formed by any distinct triple is at most a right angle, by the cosine rule (`|PQ|²+|QR|²-|PR|² >=0`). Collinearity is impossible. A triangular convex hull is impossible because its interior fourth point would have an angle at least `120°` to two vertices. Therefore the convex hull is a quadrilateral, and all four interior angles are `<=90°`; since they sum to `360°`, it is a rectangle. The two side lengths are `>=1` and its diagonal is `<=sqrt(2)`, forcing both sides exactly `1`. Hence **every global n4 optimizer is a unit square**, whose contact graph has no unit triangle. This is an independently checked elementary proof of a *known finite exception*, not eventual-n progress.

# Independent mathematical referee — Pauli’s diameter-endpoint hull theorem

**Verdict: The proposed inequality is valid for \(m\ge3\) under the stated KKT interpretation of “unstressed.” The constant \(4\sqrt n+5\) is unnecessarily weak. The case \(m=2\) requires a separate definition and proof. A stronger finite theorem follows from Reinhardt’s perimeter inequality, with improved asymptotic constants. None of these results resolves Erdős Problem #99.**

I inspected the accessible local research notes, including erdos99-verified-notes.md §225 and the Wave94, Wave100, and Wave104–105 audits. The precise new manuscript from Pauli agent 01a189e2 was not present in those files. This is therefore an independent audit of the supplied theorem and its necessary mathematical steps, rather than a line-by-line comparison with Pauli’s complete response.

## 1\. Precise hypotheses

Let \(X=\{p_1,\ldots,p_n\}\subset\mathbb R^2\) be an **unrestricted exact global minimizer** of diameter \(D=D_n\), subject to

\[
|p_i-p_j|\ge1\qquad(i\ne j).
\]

Choose any nonnegative KKT equilibrium stress, with multipliers \(\lambda_{ij}\) supported on unit contacts and \(\mu_{ij}\) supported on diameter pairs.

Normalize the diameter multipliers by

\[
\sum_{|p_i-p_j|=D}\mu_{ij}=1.
\]

Define

\[
S=\{i:\lambda_{ij}>0\text{ for at least one }j\},
\qquad z=n-|S|.
\]

Thus **unstressed means incident to no strictly positive contact multiplier**. A site can have geometric unit contacts whose KKT multipliers are zero and still count toward \(z\).

Let \(B\) contain the endpoints of all diameter pairs carrying positive \(\mu\), and let \(H=\operatorname{conv}(B)\). Write \(m\) for the number of extreme vertices of \(H\). Since \(\sum\mu=1\), some diameter pair has positive multiplier, so \(m\ge2\) and \(\operatorname{diam}(H)=D\). The same containment argument works if \(H\) is enlarged to the hull of *all* diametral endpoints, although its vertex count may change.

The KKT certificate is justified by the Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification. In the squared-diameter formulation, the scaling direction \(\dot p_i=p_i,\ \dot t=2D^2+1\) strictly decreases every active unit-separation and diameter constraint. Consequently,

\[
\sum_{j}\lambda_{ij}(p_i-p_j)
=
\sum_j\mu_{ij}(p_i-p_j)
\tag{1}
\]

at every vertex. Dotting with \(p_i\) and summing gives

\[
\sum_{ij}\lambda_{ij}=D^2.
\]

This stress formalism is also developed in Archit Das’s September 2026 **preprint**, [Stress, rigidity and rhombic reductions](https://zenodo.org/records/22768362?utm_source=chatgpt.com). It is a necessary optimality condition, not a sufficient certificate of unrestricted global optimality. [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/22768362)

## 2\. The hull-containment lemma is sound

Consider a nontrivial connected component \(C\) of the graph consisting only of positive-\(\lambda\) contact edges. Let \(B_C=B\cap C\).

**First, \(B_C\ne\varnothing\).** Otherwise the right-hand side of (1) vanishes at every vertex of \(C\). Taking the scalar product with each \(p_i\) and summing over \(i\in C\) yields

\[
0=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(C)}\lambda_{ij}|p_i-p_j|^2
  =\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(C)}\lambda_{ij}>0,
\]

a contradiction. This handles every nontrivial component individually; connectedness of the full contact graph is unnecessary.

**Second, all of \(C\) lies in \(\operatorname{conv}(B_C)\).** At a vertex with no positive diameter multiplier, (1) says

\[
p_i=\frac{\sum_j\lambda_{ij}p_j}{\sum_j\lambda_{ij}}.
\]

For every linear functional \(v\cdot p\), the values at those vertices are weighted harmonic averages of their neighbors. The discrete maximum and minimum principles place their values between those attained on \(B_C\). Applying this in every direction proves

\[
p_i\in\operatorname{conv}(B_C)\subseteq H.
\]

Taking the union of components,

\[
\boxed{S\subseteq H.}
\tag{2}
\]

This also proves containment when \(H\) is a segment. It does **not** prove that every site inside \(H\) is stressed, or that every site outside \(H\) has no geometric unit contact. Those reversals are invalid.

The earlier project note §225 records substantially this same component-containment principle. Its historical novelty is therefore not established by the present audit.

## 3\. Exact global lattice averaging

Let

\[
\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt3}=0.9068996821171089\ldots
\]

be the point density of the unit triangular lattice.

For every \(r<D/2\), each translate of the lattice has at most \(n-1\) points in the *open* disk of radius \(r\). Otherwise, selecting \(n\) such points would produce a legal configuration of diameter strictly less than \(2r<D\), contradicting exact global optimality.

Averaging the lattice count over a fundamental cell gives exactly

\[
\mathbb E\,N(r)=\frac{2\pi r^2}{\sqrt3}.
\]

Therefore \(\frac{2\pi r^2}{\sqrt3}\le n-1\) for every \(r<D/2\). Letting \(r\uparrow D/2\) proves

\[
\boxed{\alpha D^2\le n-1,\qquad
D\le\sqrt{\frac{2\sqrt3}{\pi}}\sqrt{n-1}.}
\tag{3}
\]

The constant in the last inequality is

\[
\sqrt{\frac{2\sqrt3}{\pi}}=1.050075135808664\ldots
\]

The distinction between the open-disk strict competitor and the limiting non-strict inequality is essential. No extra \(+1\), strict final inequality, or positive population reserve can be inserted merely because the finite-radius competitors are strict.

## 4\. Oler on \(H\): valid, including boundary points

Write \(A=A(H)\) and \(L=P(H)\). By (2), the \(|S|=n-z\) positively stressed original sites form a unit-separated set inside the **closed convex body** \(H\).

The correctly normalized Oler inequality is

\[
\boxed{n-z\le\frac{2A}{\sqrt3}+\frac L2+1.}
\tag{4}
\]

Its use does not require \(H\) to be the convex hull of exactly the stressed sites. Nor must the sites lie strictly inside \(H\); boundary sites are counted.

The original result is Norman Oler, *A Finite Packing Problem* (1961), DOI 10.4153/CMB-1961-018-7. The compact-convex-body statement, including the convention that a segment has twice its length as perimeter, is explicitly restated by Böröczky and Ruzsa (2007), [Note on an inequality of Wegner, p. 2](https://www.renyi.hu/~carlos/wegner.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com). [Cambridge University Press+1](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/canadian-mathematical-bulletin/article/finite-packing-problem/2145B773DA97D22970948705CC67414D?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

For \(m\ge3\), Cauchy’s perimeter bound and the polygonal isoperimetric inequality give

\[
L\le\pi D,\qquad
A\le\frac{L^2}{4m\tan(\pi/m)}
  \le\frac{\pi^2D^2}{4m\tan(\pi/m)}.
\]

Substituting into (4), then using (3), proves

\[
n-z\le
\frac{\pi}{m\tan(\pi/m)}(n-1)
+\sqrt{\frac{\pi\sqrt3}{2}}\sqrt{n-1}+1.
\]

Define

\[
q_m=\frac{\pi}{m\tan(\pi/m)},\qquad
c=\sqrt{\frac{\pi\sqrt3}{2}}
 =1.6494541661869015\ldots
\]

The exact finite conclusion is

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
z\ge(1-q_m)(n-1)-c\sqrt{n-1}
\qquad(m\ge3).}
\tag{5}
\]

Because \(0<1-q_m<1\) and \(c<2\), (5) implies Pauli’s advertised weaker inequality

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
z\ge
\left(1-\frac{\pi}{m\tan(\pi/m)}\right)n
-4\sqrt n-5.}
\tag{6}
\]

So the proposed numerical error term is safe. In fact the coefficient \(4\) may be reduced to \(1.649455\) with only a small change to the additive constant.

### Explicit checks for \(m=3,4\)

| \(m\) | \(q_m\) | \(1-q_m\) in Pauli’s bound | Stronger leading coefficient below |
| --- | --: | --: | --: |
| 3 | \(0.604599788078\) | \(0.395400211922\) | \(0.448671104578\) |
| 4 | \(\pi/4=0.785398163397\) | \(0.214601836603\) | \(0.363380227632\) |

There is no sign reversal at \(m=3\) or \(m=4\). Both proposed leading coefficients are positive and the estimates follow without a small-\(m\) exception.

## 5\. The \(m=2\) defect and its repair

**As written, (6) is undefined at \(m=2\)** because \(\tan(\pi/2)\) is not a finite real number. Assigning \(q_2=0\) by a one-sided limiting convention is harmless, but it must be stated explicitly; the polygonal isoperimetric step itself cannot be applied at \(m=2\).

When \(m=2\), \(H\) is a segment of length \(D\). By (2), every positively stressed site lies on this segment. Unit separation gives the elementary sharp packing count

\[
n-z\le\lfloor D\rfloor+1.
\]

Using (3),

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
z\ge n-1-
\left\lfloor
\sqrt{\frac{2\sqrt3}{\pi}}\sqrt{n-1}
\right\rfloor.}
\tag{7}
\]

This is considerably stronger than the formally continued \(z\ge n-4\sqrt n-5\). It also shows why exact globality matters: a long collinear unit-contact chain can be KKT-stationary with all its vertices stressed, but its diameter grows linearly with \(n\) and it is not a global minimum-diameter packing.

## 6\. A stronger asymptotic theorem

Pauli’s leading coefficient can be improved for every \(m\ge3\) by replacing the coarse \(L\le\pi D\) area estimate with the polygonal diameter-perimeter inequality, historically due to Reinhardt and discussed in Basudeb Datta, *A Discrete Isoperimetric Problem* (1997), DOI 10.1023/A:1004997002327.

For a convex \(m\)\-gon of diameter \(D\),

\[
L\le2mD\sin\frac{\pi}{2m}.
\]

Combining it with the polygonal isoperimetric inequality yields

\[
A\le
\frac m2\cos\frac{\pi}{m}
\tan\frac{\pi}{2m}\,D^2.
\]

Define

\[
\beta_m=
\frac{2m}{\pi}\cos\frac{\pi}{m}
\tan\frac{\pi}{2m}
=q_m\left(
\frac{\sin(\pi/(2m))}{\pi/(2m)}
\right)^2.
\]

Since \(\sin x<x\) for \(x>0\), **\(\beta_m<q_m\)**. The same Oler and exact-global averaging argument now proves

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
z\ge(1-\beta_m)(n-1)
-m\sin\frac{\pi}{2m}
\sqrt{\frac{2\sqrt3}{\pi}}\sqrt{n-1},
\qquad m\ge3.}
\tag{8}
\]

For \(m=3\), (8) becomes the particularly clean

\[
z\ge
\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{\pi}\right)(n-1)
-\frac32\sqrt{\frac{2\sqrt3}{\pi}}\sqrt{n-1}.
\tag{9}
\]

For \(m=4\), the exact isodiametric quadrilateral area bound \(A\le D^2/2\) is sharper still. It follows directly from \(A=\tfrac12 d_1d_2\sin\theta\) for the two diagonals, each of length at most \(D\). Hence

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
z\ge\left(1-\frac2\pi\right)(n-1)
-4\sin\frac\pi8
\sqrt{\frac{2\sqrt3}{\pi}}\sqrt{n-1}.}
\tag{10}
\]

The coefficients of \(\sqrt{n-1}\) in (9) and (10) are respectively \(1.575112703713\ldots\) and \(1.607385428850\ldots\).

For \(m\to\infty\), expansion of (8) gives

\[
1-\beta_m=\frac{5\pi^2}{12m^2}+O(m^{-4}),
\]

compared with Pauli’s

\[
1-q_m=\frac{\pi^2}{3m^2}+O(m^{-4}).
\]

Thus the improved leading deficit is **25% larger** than Pauli’s asymptotic \(m^{-2}\) coefficient. More explicitly,

\[
z\ge
\left(\frac{5\pi^2}{12m^2}+O(m^{-4})\right)(n-1)
-\bigl(1.6494541662+O(m^{-2})\bigr)\sqrt{n-1}.
\tag{11}
\]

This is a valid sharpening obtained from exact-global lattice averaging plus classical polygon geometry. It is not asserted to be historically new. The earlier local §225 bound already used the same Reinhardt geometric expression in a different \(D\)\-based form.

## 7\. Adversarial checks on the conclusions

The theorem says that a small diameter-endpoint hull forces many **stress-inactive** original sites. It does not say those sites have no unit contacts, lie outside \(H\), or can be moved simultaneously to reduce the diameter.

An exact-global counterexample to the first tempting reversal exists at \(n=8\): the regular unit-side heptagon together with an admissible interior center. Bezdek–Fodor proved its unrestricted global diameter optimality in *Minimal Diameter of Certain Sets in the Plane* (1999), DOI 10.1006/jcta.1998.2889. The heptagon sides form a triangle-free contact cycle; the center has no unit contact and lies **inside** the diameter-endpoint hull. Thus an unstressed site need not lie outside \(H\). The unit square at \(n=4\) is an even simpler exact-global triangle-free configuration with \(z=0\) for its natural symmetric stress. [ScienceDirect+1](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0097316598928898?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

There is also an explicit infinite feasible obstruction to deducing an Oler slack penalty merely from triangle-freeness. Take a full unit triangular-lattice hexagon with \(N_k=3k^2+3k+1\) sites and apply the linear stretch

\[
(x,y)\longmapsto(x,(1+k^{-4})y).
\]

All original distances remain at least one; the only surviving unit contacts are horizontal, so the original contact graph is triangle-free. The unstretched hexagonal patch has equality in Oler’s inequality, while the stretched patch has Oler slack \(O(k^{-2})\to0\). These are **not** globally optimal configurations: translated triangular-lattice disk competitors have strictly smaller diameter for sufficiently large \(k\). This refutes any uniform positive Oler surcharge for all triangle-free feasible sets, while leaving an all-global version open.

The published triangle-free penny-graph bound of Eppstein (2018, Theorem 4) is

\[
e(X)\le 2n-\sqrt{\frac{\pi\sqrt3}{2}}\sqrt n+O(1)
\]

for the total number of original unit-contact edges. It covers disconnected graphs, so no connectedness loophole is available. It is, however, an **upper** edge bound. Neither (6) nor the stronger (8) supplies the missing all-global lower edge bound that would contradict it. See [Eppstein’s original journal paper, Theorem 4, p. 493](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/EMIS/journals/JGAA/accepted/2018/463.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com). [JGAA](https://jgaa-v5.cs.brown.edu/index.php/jgaa/article/view/paper463?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

The actual structural consequences that survive are conditional: for fixed \(m\), (8) forces \(z=\Omega(n)\); if \(z=O(\sqrt n)\), then \(m=\Omega(n^{1/4})\). Both are consistent with the possibility of large triangle-free globally optimal configurations. Neither guarantees even one exact unit equilateral triangle.

## 8\. Strictness, prior work, and final disposition

Every step in the proof of (5) and (8) uses a non-strict inequality at its conclusion. Oler includes sites on the boundary of \(H\); the translated-lattice contradiction is strict before taking the radius limit; and the resulting \(\alpha D^2\le n-1\) is non-strict. Possible strictness in polygon geometry does not justify replacing any displayed \(\ge\) with \(>\) without an additional equality-case analysis. Integer rounding of \(z\) is possible after the real bound is established, but introduces no new geometric conclusion.

The key historical references are [Erdős’s original 1994 paper](https://mathematica-pannonica.ttk.pte.hu/articles/mp05-2/mp05-2-261-269.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com), Oler’s *A Finite Packing Problem* (DOI 10.4153/CMB-1961-018-7), Reinhardt’s polygon-perimeter bound as treated in Datta (1997, DOI 10.1023/A:1004997002327), [Böröczky–Ruzsa’s Oler/Groemer equality account](https://www.renyi.hu/~carlos/wegner.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [Bezdek–Fodor (1999)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0097316598928898?utm_source=chatgpt.com), [Eppstein (2018)](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/EMIS/journals/JGAA/accepted/2018/463.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com), and [Das’s 2026 preprint](https://zenodo.org/records/22768362?utm_source=chatgpt.com). The public problem remains listed as open. [Erdős Problems](https://erdosproblems.ai/problems/99?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Let \(A=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) be unit-separated with diameter \(D\), and put

\[

For a one-sided path

\[
x_i(t)=x_i+t u_i+\tfrac12t^2w_i+o(t^2),\qquad t\downarrow0,
\]

the exact expansion is

\[
|x_i(t)-x_j(t)|^2
=|r_{ij}|^2+2t\,r_{ij}\cdot u_{ij}
+t^2\bigl(|u_{ij}|^2+r_{ij}\cdot w_{ij}\bigr)+o(t^2).
\]

Write \(C=\{ij:|r_{ij}|=1\}\), \(H=\{ij:|r_{ij}|=D\}\). First-order admissibility requires

\[
r_c\cdot u_c\ge0\quad(c\in C),\qquad
r_h\cdot u_h\le0\quad(h\in H).
\]

Define

\[
C_0(u)=\{c\in C:r_c\cdot u_c=0\},\qquad
H_0(u)=\{h\in H:r_h\cdot u_h=0\}.
\]

Only these zero-rate constraints require second-order inequalities:

\[
r_c\cdot w_c\ge-|u_c|^2\quad(c\in C_0),
\qquad
r_h\cdot w_h\le-|u_h|^2\quad(h\in H_0).

Put these in \(Mw\le b\), using rows \(r_h\) for \(H_0\), rows \(-r_c\) for \(C_0\), and right-hand sides \(-|u_h|^2\), \(+|u_c|^2\), respectively. Farkas’ lemma says that \(w\) exists **if and only if** every nonnegative vector \((\alpha,\beta)\) with \((\alpha,\beta)^TM=0\) has \((\alpha,\beta)^Tb\ge0\). Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{\quad
Q_{\alpha,\beta}(u)
=\sum_{h\in H_0}\alpha_h|u_h|^2
-\sum_{c\in C_0}\beta_c|u_c|^2\le0
\quad}
\]

for every \(\alpha,\beta\ge0\) satisfying

\[
\sum_{h\in H_0}\alpha_h\nabla_x|r_h|^2
=\sum_{c\in C_0}\beta_c\nabla_x|r_c|^2.
\]

The factor \(2\) in the gradients cancels. **There is no sign error.** [people.math.carleton.ca](https://people.math.carleton.ca/~kcheung/math/notes/MATH3801/04/4_1_farkas_lemma.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

\[

\[

\[
D(t)^2\le D^2-\gamma t^2+o(t^2),\qquad \gamma>0.

\[
\boxed{\quad
Q_{\alpha,\beta}(u)+\gamma\sum_{h\in H_0}\alpha_h\le0

This is again an exact second-order linear feasibility criterion. ## Root mathematical audit: sound deductions and exact limits

**Mendel / Gauss all-global roundness, accepted as classical-consequence lemma.** For a true `n`-point global minimizer, put `D = D_n`, `K = conv(A)`, `P = perimeter(K)`, `a = area(K)`. Unit triangular-lattice Voronoi covering implies `D <= sqrt(2 sqrt(3) n / pi) + 2/sqrt(3)`, hence `n >= pi (D - 2/sqrt(3))^2/(2 sqrt(3))`. Oler gives `n <= 2a/sqrt(3) + P/2 + 1` and the perimeter-diameter bound gives `P <= pi D`. Substitution yields

`a >= pi D^2/4 - C D + eta`, with `C = 7 pi/(4 sqrt(3))` and `eta = pi/3 - sqrt(3)/2` (root verified the coefficient expansion). The **concentric-annulus** form of Bonnesen gives disks `B(z,r) subset K subset B(z,R)` with `4 pi (R-r)^2 <= P^2 - 4 pi a`, so `R-r <= sqrt(C D - eta)`. Because `r <= D/2 <= R`, for sufficiently large `D` this implies `B(z, D/2 - sqrt(CD-eta)) subset K subset B(z, D/2 + sqrt(CD-eta))` and width in every direction at least `D - 2 sqrt(CD-eta)`. The concentric hypothesis is essential: a generic inball/circumball may have different centers. Sources: Oler (1961), DOI `10.4153/CMB-1961-018-7`; Bonnesen (1924) and Fusco's survey DOI `10.1007/s13373-015-0074-x`. This restricts global hulls; it forces **no unit equilateral triangle** by itself, no useful global lower bound on diametral pairs.

**Noether strict quadratic lifting, root checked and accepted as a sufficient finite-path lemma.** At an admissible first-order velocity `u`, let `C0` and `H0` be the unit contacts and diametral pairs with zero first-order rate. If some acceleration `w` and `gamma>0` satisfy `r_c·w_c + |u_c|^2 >= 0` for every `c in C0` and `r_h·w_h + |u_h|^2 <= -gamma` for every `h in H0`, then the polynomial `x_i + t u_i + t² w_i/2` has at worst cubic negative contact errors and strictly improves every active diameter at order `t` or `t²`. Uniform dilation by `1+K t³` for large fixed `K` repairs all contact errors while preserving strict diameter improvement; inactive inequalities stay strict. This is a **real same-n improvement**; a global optimizer cannot admit the certificate.

For a normalized equilibrium stress on `C0,H0` with nonnegative `alpha_h,beta_c`, `sum alpha_h = 1`, the position dot product proves `sum beta_c = D²`. Thus the stress polytope `Sigma(u)` is compact. Define `Q_sigma(u) = sum_H alpha_h |u_h|² - sum_C beta_c |u_c|²`. By the linear Farkas alternative, `Sigma(u)=empty` or `max_{sigma in Sigma(u)} Q_sigma(u)<0` implies an acceleration with `gamma>0` and therefore a true descent. The direction and normalization of signs were independently checked. At an exact local minimizer, first-order KKT stresses exist and complementarity with any admissible `u` places their support in `C0,H0`; consequently `Sigma(u)` is nonempty and `max Q >= 0` for **every** admissible `u`. **Missing:** prove that every sufficiently large triangle-free *unrestricted exact global optimizer* admits the unfavorable-to-optimality `u`. Neither a single stress nor a weak fixed-diameter second-order feasibility system is enough.

**Noether higher-order finite jet, provisional beyond sufficient direction.** The uniform `t^(m+1)` dilation clearly establishes sufficiency if all active diametral gaps have positive leading coefficients by order `m` and contact gaps have no negative leading coefficients through `m`. The proposed converse using Nash analytic curve selection is plausible but was **not separately root-refereed**, including the necessary parameterization and truncation assumptions. No uniform order or global theorem is provided.

**Wegener stress-kernel conditional reduction, NOT independently certified.** The formal differentiation identity for a smooth fixed-contact/diameter exact-optimum arc follows from equilibrium: `sum_C lambda |v_c|² - sum_H mu |v_h|² = 0`. The stronger deduction `v_x,v_y in ker Omega` depends on a **PSD** hypothesis for `Omega=L(lambda)-L(mu)`; ordinary KKT stationarity does not make that signed Laplacian PSD on the entire ambient space. Given PSD, and Das's appropriately scoped connected-component estimate `c <= 2k`, rank subadditivity supplies `dim ker Omega <= n-s+c+k <= n-s+3k`. The source's exact PSD hypotheses and spine-component definitions still require independent formal/theorem-level verification. Furthermore, `h(n)=infinity` guarantees a positive-dimensional optimum stratum **somewhere** but cannot rule out an isolated triangle-free optimizer coexisting with a triangle-bearing continuum. Eventual `h(n)<infinity` would be sufficient through Stewart, but is unproved and is not logically necessary for the original statement.

**W109_1011, Euclid, and original finite exceptions.** The second-order Farkas signs from 1011 are correct only for appropriately selected first-order admissible zero-rate constraints; a formal weak quadratic feasibility test does not automatically produce a finite motion. The bulk-shear Oler defect asymptotic holds for the patch family examined and cannot be extrapolated to all global minimizers. The unit rhombus family with angle `theta` from 60 to 90 degrees has `D(theta)=2 cos(theta/2)` *decreasing* while its Oler defect increases: a direct counterexample to any monotone diameter-penalty claim. The regular unit-side heptagon plus interior center is a **global** triangle-free optimizer for **n=8 only**, by Bezdek–Fodor (1999), DOI `10.1006/jcta.1998.2889`. Perturbing/rescaling any fixed-n optimizer yields triangle-free configurations with one contact and diameters approaching `D_n`, so there is **no positive minimum-diameter gap over all triangle-free near-minimizers**. ## Independent primary-source verification of Bonnesen transfer

Source: **T. Bonnesen (1924)**, as precisely stated in **Nicola Fusco, "The quantitative isoperimetric inequality and related topics," Bulletin of Mathematical Sciences 5 (2015), Theorem 1.1**, https://doi.org/10.1007/s13373-015-0074-x . For any planar convex body of area `A` and perimeter `P`, there exist **concentric** inscribed and enclosing circles of radii `r_- <= r_+` satisfying

`(r_+ - r_-)^2 <= (P^2 - 4*pi*A)/(4*pi)`.

This *specific concentric-annulus* inequality is independently source-verified. It is distinct from the familiar inradius/circumradius inequality `P^2-4*pi*A >= pi^2*(R-r)^2`, which need not assert that the extrema share a center.

Let `D=D_n` be the diameter of any original exact global optimizer with `n` sufficiently large; `H=conv(X)`, `A=area(H)`, `P=perimeter(H)`. Using the root-reviewed W110_1017 Fourier/Oler result with `c=3^(5/4)/(160*pi)>0`,

`n >= pi*D^2/(2*sqrt(3)) + c*sqrt(D)`.

Oler's inequality `n <= (2/sqrt(3))*A+P/2+1`, Cauchy's `P <= pi*D`, and isodiametric `A <= pi*D^2/4` imply

`A >= pi*D^2/4 - (pi*sqrt(3)/4)*D + (sqrt(3)*c/2)*sqrt(D) - sqrt(3)/2`.

Substitute this lower bound in `P^2-4*pi*A` and use `P<=pi*D`: the isoperimetric deficit obeys

`0 <= P^2 - 4*pi*A <= pi^2*sqrt(3)*D - 2*pi*sqrt(3)*c*sqrt(D) + 2*pi*sqrt(3)`.

Bonnesen yields **concentric** disks with

`r_+ - r_- <= sqrt((pi*sqrt(3)/4)*D - (sqrt(3)*c/2)*sqrt(D) + sqrt(3)/2) = O(sqrt(D))`.

Since an inscribed disk has diameter `2*r_- <= D` and any enclosing disk satisfies `2*r_+ >= D`, these disks sandwich `H` between concentric disks of radii at least `D/2-O(sqrt(D))` and at most `D/2+O(sqrt(D))`. The same inequalities give a valid near-maximal *perimeter* estimate using the isoperimetric upper bound `A<=P^2/(4*pi)`:

`P >= (sqrt(4*pi^2*D^2 + 3*pi^2 + 8*pi*sqrt(3)*c*sqrt(D) - 8*pi*sqrt(3)) - pi*sqrt(3))/2`,

and hence `pi*D-P <= pi*sqrt(3)/2 - sqrt(3)*c/sqrt(D) + O(1/D)` for large D. (The exact radical bound, rather than the asymptotic truncation, is the certified assertion.) This perimeter formula was not previously source-verified in the Wave110 root report and is now independently derived from the stated established inequalities.

### 1\. Exact second-order dual statement

Let \(A=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)\), with minimum separation \(1\), squared diameter \(s=D^2\), original contact set

\[
C=\{ij:|p_i-p_j|=1\},
\]

and complete active-diameter set

\[
H=\{ij:|p_i-p_j|=D\}.
\]

Define

\[
B_{ij}(u)=(p_i-p_j)\cdot(u_i-u_j).
\]

A first-order critical velocity satisfies

\[
B_c(u)\ge0\quad(c\in C),\qquad
B_h(u)\le0\quad(h\in H).
\]

At every local minimum, the epigraph formulation with constraints \(1-|p_i-p_j|^2\le0\) and \(|p_i-p_j|^2-s\le0\) satisfies MFCQ: the direction \(\dot p_i=p_i,\ \dot s=2s+1\) strictly decreases every active constraint.

Consequently, nonnegative multipliers \(\lambda_c,\mu_h\) exist with

\[
\sum_{h\in H}\mu_h=1,\qquad
\sum_{c\in C}\lambda_c=D^2,
\]

and equilibrium

\[
\sum_{c\in C}\lambda_c B_c(v)
=
\sum_{h\in H}\mu_h B_h(v)
\quad\text{for every }v.
\]

Substitute a critical \(u\). The left side is nonnegative; the right side is nonpositive. Both must vanish. Therefore every positively weighted contact and diameter has zero first-order rate.

**Thus a zero-rate normalized equilibrium stress always exists.** In fact, every normalized equilibrium stress has zero-rate support for every critical \(u\).

Define

\[
Q_\sigma(u)=
\sum_{h\in H}\mu_h|u_i-u_j|^2
-
\sum_{c\in C}\lambda_c|u_i-u_j|^2.
\]

For zero-rate pairs, a quadratic path

\[
p_i(t)=p_i+t u_i+\tfrac12t^2a_i
\]

strictly improves the squared diameter by \(\varepsilon t^2\) if

\[
B_c(a)+|u_i-u_j|^2>0,
\]

and

\[
B_h(a)+|u_i-u_j|^2<-\varepsilon.
\]

The strict linear Farkas alternative says these acceleration inequalities are feasible precisely when the corresponding nonnegative equilibrium certificates satisfy

\[
Q_\sigma(u)<-\varepsilon.
\]

A contact-only nonnegative equilibrium certificate is impossible: testing equilibrium against radial dilation yields \(\sum_c\lambda_c=0\). Hence every nonzero dual certificate has positive diameter mass and can be normalized.

The normalized stress set is compact. Therefore

\[
\boxed{\max_{\sigma\in\Sigma(u)}Q_\sigma(u)<0}
\]

gives a strict quadratic acceleration and, for sufficiently small positive \(t\), an **actual feasible same-\(n\) decrease in diameter**. Strict inequalities absorb all higher-order terms.

It follows that every local, hence every global, optimizer satisfies

\[
\boxed{\forall u\text{ critical},\quad
\max_{\sigma\in\Sigma(u)}Q_\sigma(u)\ge0.}
\]

This is consistent with the classical second-order tensegrity duality of Connelly and Whiteley (1996), [Second-Order Rigidity and Prestress Stability](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/S0895480192229236?utm_source=chatgpt.com). [SIAM](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/S0895480192229236)

### 2\. Arbitrarily large dense-contact obstruction

Let \(m=2k+1\) be sufficiently large and odd. Set

\[
\alpha=\frac{\pi}{m},\qquad
R=\frac1{2\sin\alpha},\qquad
p_j=R(\cos(2j\alpha),\sin(2j\alpha)).
\]

The \(m\) rim vertices form a regular polygon with all neighboring distances exactly \(1\). Its maximum distance is

\[
D=2R\cos(\alpha/2)=\frac{\cos(\alpha/2)}{\sin\alpha}.
\]

The complete rim contact set consists of \(m\) sides \(j,j+1\), and the complete rim diameter set consists of \(m\) longest chords \(j,j+k\). These diameter directions are spaced by \(\pi/m\) modulo \(\pi\).

Inside the disk of radius \(R-3\), insert the sites of the rhombic lattice

\[
L_m=\mathbb Z v+\mathbb Z w,\qquad
v=(1,0),\quad
w=(\cos\phi,\sin\phi),\quad
\phi=\pi/3+1/m.
\]

Its only unit vectors are \(\pm v,\pm w\). Indeed, when integer coefficients have the same sign, every other combination has squared length at least \(2\). For opposite signs,

\[
|av-bw|^2=(a-b)^2+2ab(1-\cos\phi)>1
\quad(a,b\ge1).
\]

Thus the interior unit-contact graph is a subgraph of the bipartite square grid. There are no rim-to-interior contacts because the radial gap is at least \(3\).

All interior-interior distances are at most \(2R-6\), and rim-interior distances at most \(2R-3<D\). Hence **every active diameter remains one of the \(m\) rim longest chords**.

The full configuration \(A_m\) is triangle-free on its original sites.

Writing \(I_m\) for its interior population, fundamental parallelogram cells have area \(\sin\phi\) and lie within distance \(1\) of their centers. The cell covering bounds give

\[
\frac{\pi(R-4)^2}{\sin\phi}
\le I_m\le
\frac{\pi(R-2)^2}{\sin\phi}
\]

for sufficiently large \(m\).

Since \(\sin\phi=\sqrt3/2+O(1/m)\) and \(R=\Theta(m)\),

\[
n_m=m+I_m
=\frac{\pi}{2\sqrt3}D^2+O(D).
\]

All but \(O(R)\) interior sites have four unit neighbors, so the number of original unit contacts is

\[
\boxed{|C(A_m)|=2n_m-O(D)=2n_m-O(\sqrt{n_m}).}
\]

This is a dense triangle-free contact framework, compatible with Eppstein’s published triangle-free penny-graph bounds. [JGA&A](https://jgaa-v5.cs.brown.edu/index.php/jgaa/article/view/paper463?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

### 3\. Every normalized stress ignores the dense interior

Place positive multipliers on all rim constraints:

\[
\mu_{j,j+k}=\frac1m,\qquad
\lambda_{j,j+1}=\frac{D^2}{m},
\]

and zero contact multipliers on the interior.

These satisfy equilibrium because

\[
\sum_{\text{two rim sides at }j}(p_j-p_\ell)
=2(1-\cos2\alpha)p_j,
\]

while

\[
\sum_{\text{two longest chords at }j}(p_j-p_\ell)
=2(1-\cos2k\alpha)p_j,
\]

and their coefficient ratio is

\[
\frac{1-\cos2k\alpha}{1-\cos2\alpha}=D^2.
\]

More strongly, **every nonnegative equilibrium stress vanishes on every interior contact**. There are no active diameter pairs incident to an interior site. Summing interior equilibrium equations against the positions gives

\[
\sum_{c\in C_{\mathrm{interior}}}\lambda_c|p_i-p_j|^2=0.
\]

Each summand is nonnegative and each contact length is \(1\), so every interior \(\lambda_c=0\).

The exact unit contacts of the dense interior are therefore all **unstressed**, regardless of how many there are.

### 4\. The rim has no nonrigid first-order critical velocity

It remains to check rigidity, rather than assume it.

Write a rim velocity in radial/tangential components:

\[
u_j=e^{2ij\alpha}(a_j+i b_j).
\]

For a chord of step \(s\), its zero-rate equation is

\[
(1-\cos2s\alpha)(a_j+a_{j+s})
+\sin2s\alpha(b_{j+s}-b_j)=0.
\]

Use Fourier modes \(a_j=A z^j,\ b_j=B z^j\), where \(z=e^{2\pi i\ell/m}\). For the two step sizes \(s=1,k\), a nonzero mode requires

\[
\frac{\tan\alpha}{\tan(k\alpha)}
=
\frac{\tan(\ell\alpha)}{\tan(k\ell\alpha)}.
\]

Because \(k\alpha=\pi/2-\alpha/2\), the left side is \(\tan\alpha\tan(\alpha/2)>0\).

For odd \(\ell\), the right side is

\[
\tan(\ell\alpha)\tan(\ell\alpha/2),
\]

which equals the left side only at \(\ell=1\): it is strictly increasing before \(\ell\alpha=\pi/2\) and negative afterward.

For even \(\ell\), the right side is

\[
-\tan(\ell\alpha)\cot(\ell\alpha/2),
\]

which is negative before \(\ell\alpha=\pi/2\) and strictly decreasing from \(+\infty\) to its endpoint value afterward. Equality occurs only at \(\ell=m-1\).

The zero mode gives rotation. The modes \(\ell=1,m-1\) give translations. Therefore the complete rim side-plus-longest-chord framework has only the three Euclidean infinitesimal motions.

Now let \(u\) be *any* first-order critical velocity of the full configuration. Positive rim multipliers force **every rim side and every rim diameter to have zero rate**. The Fourier calculation implies

\[
u_j=t+\omega Jp_j
\]

at every rim vertex.

Since every normalized equilibrium stress is supported on the rim,

\[
Q_\sigma(u)
=\omega^2\left(D^2\sum_h\mu_h-\sum_c\lambda_c\right)=0.
\]

Consequently,

\[
\boxed{\forall u\text{ critical},\
\forall\sigma\in\Sigma(u),\ Q_\sigma(u)=0.}
\]

There is always a zero-rate stress, and the maximum quadratic form is exactly zero. **Both proposed descent alternatives fail throughout this infinite family.**

Positive equilibrium and infinitesimal rigidity also prove ordinary local diameter minimality. If arbitrarily close noncongruent feasible rim perturbations had diameter at most \(D\), align them by translation and rotation, normalize their displacements, and take a convergent subsequence. The limit would be a nonzero critical infinitesimal motion orthogonal to rigid motions, contradicting the Fourier result. Interior movements may preserve the diameter, so the full configuration is locally minimal but need not be strict.

The family does not supply counterexamples to Erdős #99.

Let \(\Delta=\sqrt3/2\). The interior cell bound gives

\[
n_m\le m+\frac{\pi(R-2)^2}{\Delta}.
\]

A translated unit triangular lattice inside the **open** disk of radius \(D/2\) has, for some translation, at least its mean population

\[
\frac{\pi D^2}{4\Delta}
=\frac{\pi R^2\cos^2(\alpha/2)}{\Delta}.

The competitor population exceeds the displayed upper bound on \(n_m\) whenever

### 1\. Proved: exact semialgebraic multiplicity dichotomy

For each fixed \(n\ge3\), let \(D_n\) be the unrestricted globally minimum diameter under unit separation. Represent a labeled configuration by its squared-distance vector

\[
q=(q_{ij})_{i<j},\qquad q_{ij}=|p_i-p_j|^2.
\]

Define the \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) matrix

\[
G(q)_{ij}=\frac{q_{1i}+q_{1j}-q_{ij}}2,\qquad 2\le i,j\le n.
\]

A vector \(q\) represents a planar configuration, up to Euclidean isometry, precisely when \(G(q)\succeq0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}G(q)\le2\). This is the standard Euclidean-distance-matrix characterization. [CWI](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/2111/2111D.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Consider

\[
\mathcal F_n(t)=
\left\{q:
1\le q_{ij}\le t,\quad
G(q)\succeq0,\quad \operatorname{rank}G(q)\le2
\right\}.
\]

All conditions are polynomial equalities or inequalities with rational coefficients. Feasibility is monotone in \(t\), so

\[
\{t:\mathcal F_n(t)\ne\varnothing\}=[D_n^2,\infty).
\]

Compactness proves attainment. Tarski–Seidenberg quantifier elimination makes this ray semialgebraic over \(\mathbb Q\); therefore **\(D_n^2\) is a real algebraic number**.

Consequently,

\[
\mathcal M_n=\mathcal F_n(D_n^2)
\]

is a compact semialgebraic set over the real algebraic numbers. It represents all labeled exact global optimizers modulo Euclidean isometries. Relabeling acts by a finite permutation group, so finiteness of \(\mathcal M_n\) is equivalent to \(h(n)<\infty\).

Define its triangle-free locus

\[
\mathcal T_n=
\left\{q\in\mathcal M_n:
\forall i<j<k,\ 
(q_{ij}-1)^2+(q_{ik}-1)^2+(q_{jk}-1)^2>0
\right\}.
\]

This is relatively open and semialgebraic.

**Exact dichotomy.** If \(h(n)=\infty\) and \(\mathcal T_n\ne\varnothing\), exactly one of the following holds:

1. \(\mathcal T_n\) is infinite. It then has positive semialgebraic dimension and contains a nonconstant semialgebraic analytic arc of **exact, globally optimal, triangle-free** configurations.
2. \(\mathcal T_n\) is finite. Every one of its points is isolated in the full optimizer space \(\mathcal M_n\), has algebraic squared-distance coordinates, and is separated by a positive distance in squared-distance space from all triangle-containing optimizers.

**Proof.** A zero-dimensional semialgebraic set is finite; an infinite one contains a positive-dimensional cell and hence a nonconstant semialgebraic arc. Because \(\mathcal T_n\) is relatively open, a finite \(\mathcal T_n\) consists of isolated points of \(\mathcal M_n\). Its points have algebraic coordinates by Tarski's transfer principle. Its complement is compact, giving positive separation. This establishes both alternatives. [Taboege+1](https://taboege.de/research/dissert.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

An additional consequence is that **whenever any triangle-free global optimizer exists at fixed \(n\), an algebraic triangle-free global optimizer exists**. This follows by transferring the nonempty semialgebraic system to the real algebraic numbers.

Thus fixed-\(n\) global optimality, triangle-freeness, finiteness of \(h(n)\), and isolation are all decidable in principle by real quantifier elimination. There is no resulting uniform-in-\(n\) theorem.

- Opposite distances: \(2\).
- Same-parity distances: \(\sqrt3(1+t)\) or \(\sqrt3(1-t)\).

In the stated interval, the adjacent distances are the minimum and opposite distances the maximum. After rescaling by \((1+3t^2)^{-1/2}\), the configuration is still unit-separated and triangle-free, but has diameter

\[
\frac{2}{\sqrt{1+3t^2}}<2.
\]

This is an exact second-order descent from a configuration satisfying **strictly positive normalized equilibrium-stress equations, PSD, and maximal affine kernel**. The nontrivial infinitesimal motion is \(v_j=(-1)^ju_j\).

The hexagon is **not globally optimal**, so this does not refute a theorem that separately assumes global optimality. It rigorously refutes treating those spectral and equilibrium conditions alone as a rigidity, isolation, or optimality certificate. In the standard constrained minimization formulation, the point-coordinate Hessian of the Lagrangian is proportional to \(-\Omega\); PSD of \(\Omega\) is not a positive second-order sufficiency condition.

### 3\. Exact disconnected-minimum countermodel

Even a positive-definite Hessian at an isolated global minimum does not prevent a separate positive-dimensional global-minimum component.

Consider the nonnegative polynomial

\[
f(x,y)=(x^2+y^2)\big((x-3)^2+y^2-1\big)^2.
\]

Its global minimum is zero, attained exactly on

\[
\{(0,0)\}\ \cup\ \{(x-3)^2+y^2=1\}.
\]

The origin is an isolated global minimizer with

\[
\nabla^2 f(0,0)=128I\succ0,
\]

while the other component is a circle. The polynomial predicate

\[
(x-3)^2+y^2-1=0
\]

holds throughout the circle and fails at the isolated optimum.

This is a rigorous counterexample to any proposed inference based solely on compact semialgebraicity, disconnected optimal components, or positive local second-order curvature. It is **not** a realization of the Erdős packing problem; additional packing geometry would be needed to prohibit the corresponding configuration.

### 5\. Precise remaining gap

The semialgebraic analysis reduces the infinite-multiplicity branch to two genuinely different possibilities: a positive-dimensional triangle-free optimizer stratum, or finitely many isolated triangle-free optimizer components alongside other continuous optimal families.

The PSD/kernel example shows why stress positivity and affine-kernel rank alone cannot eliminate either possibility. To exclude isolated triangle-free optimizers for all large \(n\), one needs a **packing-specific global component theorem** or a rigorously localized version of Stewart's argument replacing global finiteness of \(h(n)\) by isolation of the particular optimizer. **Status:** The semialgebraic dichotomy, algebraicity consequences, and two counterexamples above are proved at their stated scopes. No unconditional proof or disproof of the original unrestricted Erdős #99 follows.

**Result: two rigorous global comparison bounds, an explicit stationary-but-nonoptimal family, and an infinite triangle-free candidate family. Erdős #99 remains open.** The results below apply to the original unrestricted diameter problem. The elementary deductions are self-contained; I do not claim priority for them.

Write \(D_n\) for the smallest diameter of \(n\) planar points separated by at least \(1\). Define

\[
c=\sqrt{\frac{2\sqrt3}{\pi}}=1.0500751358\ldots,
\qquad
g=\pi c=\sqrt{2\pi\sqrt3}=3.2989083324\ldots.
\]

**First, a universal comparison bound is**

\[
\boxed{D_n\le c\sqrt n\qquad(n\ge2).}
\tag{1}
\]

To prove it, take the unit triangular lattice \(\Lambda\), whose fundamental area is \(\sqrt3/2\). Set \(R=\sqrt{n\sqrt3/(2\pi)}\). Averaging over translations of \(\Lambda\), the expected number of lattice sites in a disk of radius \(R\) is

\[
\frac{\pi R^2}{\sqrt3/2}=n.
\]

Some translation therefore puts at least \(n\) lattice sites in the disk. Selecting \(n\) gives unit separation and diameter at most \(2R=c\sqrt n\). This proves (1), with no asymptotic error.

This bound yields a global invariant that excludes large analogues of the flat \(n=8\) heptagon construction. Let \(h(A)\) be the number of vertices of the convex hull of any *exact global minimizer* \(A\). Consecutive hull vertices are at least unit distance apart, so \(h(A)\le P(\operatorname{conv}A)\), where \(P\) denotes perimeter. Cauchy's perimeter formula gives \(P(K)=\int_0^\pi w_\phi(K)\,d\phi\le\pi\operatorname{diam}(K)\). Consequently,

\[
\boxed{h(A)\le g\sqrt n,\qquad
n-h(A)\ge n-g\sqrt n.}
\tag{2}
\]

In particular, an exact minimizer with **at most one interior original site has \(n\le12\)**. For \(n=13\), the inequality \(n-1\le g\sqrt n\) already fails, and the failure persists for larger \(n\). A minimizer with every site on its hull must have \(n\le10\).

There is a useful extension. Repeatedly remove the convex-hull vertices of the remaining sites, and let \(L\) be the number of peeling layers. Each layer contains at most \(\pi D_n\) sites, because its diameter is at most \(D_n\). Therefore

\[
\boxed{L\ge\frac{\sqrt n}{g}>0.3031\sqrt n.}
\tag{3}
\]

Every exact optimizer with \(n\ge44\) thus requires at least three convex layers; no fixed number of polygonal rings can remain optimal indefinitely. These conclusions use only global diameter comparison and elementary convex geometry, with no contact count, local rigidity, or stationarity assumption.

**Second, every sufficiently large subset of a unit square lattice is globally excluded, even if it satisfies first-order optimality conditions.** Suppose \(A\) is contained in a translated or rotated copy of \(\mathbb Z^2\), has \(n\) sites, and has diameter \(D\). Put \(K=\operatorname{conv}A\), and place an axis-aligned unit square \(Q\) around each site. Their interiors are disjoint, and all lie in \(K+Q\). Hence

\[
\begin{aligned}
n&\le\operatorname{area}(K+Q)\\
 &=\operatorname{area}(K)+w_x(K)+w_y(K)+1\\
 &\le\frac{\pi D^2}{4}+2D+1.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]

The middle equality follows by successively adding horizontal and vertical unit segments; the last inequality is the isodiametric inequality and \(w_x,w_y\le D\).

If this \(A\) were globally optimal, substituting (1) into (4) would give

\[
\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)n\le2c\sqrt n+1.
\]

The positive root of the associated quadratic in \(\sqrt n\) has square \(260.442956\ldots\). Thus

\[
\boxed{\text{No exact global optimizer with }n\ge261
\text{ lies in a unit square lattice.}}
\tag{5}
\]

For *complete* square grids the exclusion is stronger. The \((k+1)\times(k+1)\) grid has \(n=(k+1)^2\) and diameter \(k\sqrt2\). For every \(k\ge3\),

\[
k\sqrt2>c(k+1)\ge D_{(k+1)^2},
\]

so it is not globally optimal. The remaining \(k=2\) case, the \(3\times3\) grid, has diameter \(2\sqrt2\); nine points comprising a unit-edge regular octagon and its center have diameter \(\csc(\pi/8)=2.6131259\ldots<2\sqrt2\). Therefore **every complete square grid of at least \(3\times3\) sites fails global optimality**.

Yet these grids satisfy the first-order Karush–Kuhn–Tucker equations. Formulate the problem by minimizing \(T\) subject to \(1-|p_i-p_j|^2\le0\) and \(|p_i-p_j|^2-T\le0\). On the grid \(\{0,\ldots,k\}^2\), assign multiplier \(1/2\) to each of its two corner-to-corner diameter constraints and multiplier \(k/2\) to each unit edge along the outer perimeter, all other multipliers being zero. At every corner, the diagonal force is cancelled by the two perimeter forces; perimeter forces cancel at other boundary vertices; interior vertices carry zero force. The \(T\)\-derivative is \(1-1/2-1/2=0\). All multipliers are nonnegative. This is an explicit stationary certificate for globally inferior configurations.

**Third, the exact \(n=8\) obstruction survives, as it must.** Bezdek–Fodor proved

\[
D_8=\frac1{2\sin(\pi/14)}=2.2469796037\ldots,
\]

attained by a unit-edge regular heptagon with a suitable eighth point inside. Let the heptagon's circumradius be \(R=1/(2\sin(\pi/7))=1.1523824355\ldots\). Place its eighth site \(q\) anywhere in the open disk \(|q|<R-1\) around the center. For every heptagon vertex \(v\),

\[
1<R-|q|\le|v-q|\le R+|q|<2R-1<D_8.
\]

The seven outer sites have unit distances only between adjacent vertices. The eighth site has none. Hence this is an **open two-dimensional family of exact unrestricted global optimizers with no original unit equilateral triangle**. The global bound (2) excludes its one-interior-site architecture for \(n\ge13\), but cannot exclude an isolated freely moving interior site when many other interior sites exist. That is a precise surviving gap. [ScienceDirect+1](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0097316598928898?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

For an infinite triangle-free test family closer to the triangular-density limit, take integers \(k\ge2\), put

\[
\theta_k=\frac{\pi}{3}+k^{-3},\quad
u=(1,0),\quad v_k=(\cos\theta_k,\sin\theta_k),
\]

and define

\[
A_k=(\mathbb Zu+\mathbb Zv_k)\cap\overline B(0,k),
\qquad n_k=|A_k|.
\tag{6}
\]

Every nonzero lattice displacement \(iu+jv_k\) has length at least \(1\). Indeed, when \(ij\ge0\) this is immediate from \(i^2+j^2+2ij\cos\theta_k\); when \(ij<0\), putting \(p=|i|,q=|j|\) gives

\[
|iu+jv_k|^2
=p^2+q^2-2pq\cos\theta_k
>p^2+q^2-pq\ge1.
\]

The only unit displacements are \(\pm u,\pm v_k\), which cannot form a three-edge cycle. Since \(0,u,v_k\in A_k\), the minimum distance is exactly \(1\). **Every \(A_k\) is triangle-free at its original sites.**

Its lattice covolume is \(\kappa_k=\sin\theta_k=\sqrt3/2+O(k^{-3})\). A centered fundamental parallelogram has covering radius \(\rho_k\le\sqrt3/2\), so cell containment gives the explicit bounds

\[
\frac{\pi(k-\rho_k)^2}{\kappa_k}
\le n_k\le
\frac{\pi(k+\rho_k)^2}{\kappa_k}.
\tag{7}
\]

Thus \(n_k=(2\pi/\sqrt3)k^2+O(k)\) and \(\operatorname{diam}(A_k)\le2k\). Oler's inequality, in unit-separation normalization,

\[
n\le\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\operatorname{area}(K)
+\frac12P(K)+1
\le\frac{\pi D^2}{2\sqrt3}+\frac{\pi D}{2}+1,
\]

then implies \(D_{n_k}\ge2k-O(1)\). Therefore these triangle-free configurations are within an additive \(O(1)\) of the unrestricted optimal diameter. The derivation is rigorous, but **near-optimality does not certify global optimality**. [Rényi Institute](https://www.renyi.hu/~carlos/wegner.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

This family also adversarially defeats a proposed combinatorial contradiction based on a fixed packing-density penalty for absence of unit triangles. Its leading density equals the triangular-lattice limit even though its unit-contact graph has no triangles. Any universal positive density gap for triangle-free configurations is consequently false. Likewise, the family has many convex layers, so a claim that triangle-free configurations must have few layers is false. The layer bound (3) and lattice exclusions (5) identify genuine global restrictions, but cannot by themselves force an exact unit triangle.

To turn (6), or another infinite triangle-free family, into a disproof of the original Erdős #99, the indispensable missing certificate is

\[
\forall k\text{ in an infinite index set},\quad
\forall B\subset\mathbb R^2,\quad
|B|=n_k,\ \min_{x\ne y\in B}|x-y|\ge1
\ \Longrightarrow\
\operatorname{diam}(B)\ge\operatorname{diam}(A_k).
\]

Neither Oler's lower bound nor stationarity supplies this exact unrestricted comparison. The 2026 Das preprint already gives related rhombic-lattice and stress restrictions; I make no novelty claim for that general direction. The quantitative square-lattice and convex-layer deductions above specify what the elementary global comparison actually proves, and where the exact boundary obstruction remains. ## ROOT check of worker 1018: sharp separation of diametral directions

Original public worker `w110_1018_diameter_isolation_falsification`, UUID `d248347f-74c8-4b30-81a3-009cb0cabf5e`. The following proof has now been reconstructed by ROOT rather than credited as an independent new discovery.

Let finite unit-separated `X` have diameter `D >= 1`, and choose a diametral pair `p=(0,0), q=(D,0)`. For any third site `x=(t,s)` the diameter constraints give `2Dt >= t^2+s^2 >= 1` and `2D(D-t) >= (D-t)^2+s^2 >= 1`. Thus the vectors `x-p` and `q-x` each make angle at most `pi/2-alpha` with `q-p`, where `alpha=arcsin(1/(2D))`. For directions within `alpha` of `q-p`, the extreme projections are those of `p` and `q`, uniquely in the open angular interval, and the width is `D cos(theta)`.

If two distinct *unoriented* diametral directions differed by projective angle `delta < 2alpha`, bisect their directions. Each pair projects to the full width `D cos(delta/2)`, while the first pair uniquely provides both support extrema in that bisector direction. The pairs would coincide, contradiction. Distinct diametral directions therefore have separation at least `2alpha` on the projective angle circle of length `pi`, giving

`number of diametral pairs <= floor(pi/(2 arcsin(1/(2D)))) = O(D)`.

The constant is sharp for the admissible triple `p=(0,0)`, `q=(D,0)`, `x=(1/(2D), -sqrt(1-1/(4D^2)))`: `|p-x|=1` and `|p-q|=|q-x|=D`; angle between the distinct diameter directions equals `2alpha`. ROOT algebraically checked the squared distances and the angular identity `cos(2alpha)=1-1/(2D^2)`. This is an upper bound on diametral pairs, **not** a lower bound for every exact global optimizer. The worker's generic near-lattice perturbations illustrate why rough roundness alone cannot provide that missing lower bound; their global *exact* optimality is not claimed.

### 1\. Semialgebraic structure of all exact global optima

Let

\[
D_n=\min_{\substack{|X|=n\\ \operatorname{sep}(X)\ge1}}
\operatorname{diam}(X).
\]

Let \(\mathcal M_n\) denote the space of all **exact globally optimal** configurations, modulo Euclidean isometries, with finitely many label choices retained where convenient.

Translation and rotation can be fixed by requiring

\[
x_1=(0,0),\qquad x_2=(r,0),\quad r\ge1.
\]

The remaining constraints are polynomial:

\[
1\le\|x_i-x_j\|^2\le D_n^2.
\]

Consequently, \(\mathcal M_n\) has a compact semialgebraic representation. It admits a finite stratification into connected Nash manifolds.

Moreover,

\[
h(n)=\infty
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\dim\mathcal M_n\ge1.
\]

The implication uses the fact that a zero-dimensional semialgebraic set is finite, while the residual labeling and reflection symmetries are finite.

But **positive dimension somewhere does not imply positive dimension near every optimizer**. Isolated points can coexist with curves and higher-dimensional components. These are standard consequences of semialgebraic stratification; see Michel Coste's original lecture notes. [indico.ictp.it](https://indico.ictp.it/event/a02455/session/9/contribution/6/material/0/0.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

### 2\. Conditional theorem: analytic-stratum triangle propagation

Define the original unit-triangle locus

\[
\mathcal T_n=
\left\{X\in\mathcal M_n:
\exists\,i<j<k,\quad
\|x_i-x_j\|=\|x_j-x_k\|=\|x_k-x_i\|=1
\right\}.
\]

For each triple \(I=\{i,j,k\}\), put

\[
F_I(X)=
(\|x_i-x_j\|^2-1)^2+
(\|x_j-x_k\|^2-1)^2+
(\|x_k-x_i\|^2-1)^2.
\]

Then

\[
\mathcal T_n=\bigcup_I\{F_I=0\},
\]

so \(\mathcal T_n\) is closed and semialgebraic.

**Theorem (analytic-stratum propagation).** Fix \(n\), and let

\[
\mathcal M_n=\bigsqcup_{\alpha=1}^{m}S_\alpha
\]

be a finite stratification into connected Nash manifolds.

Suppose that, for each stratum \(S_\alpha\) of dimension \(d_\alpha\ge1\),

\[
\mathcal H^{d_\alpha}(\mathcal T_n\cap S_\alpha)>0,
\]

where \(\mathcal H^{d_\alpha}\) is Hausdorff measure.

Then **every nonisolated configuration in \(\mathcal M_n\) contains an original unit equilateral triangle**.

If, additionally, every isolated configuration contains such a triangle, then every exact global optimizer does.

**Proof.**

Fix a positive-dimensional connected stratum \(S\), of dimension \(d\).

There are finitely many triples \(I\). Since

\[
\mathcal T_n\cap S
=\bigcup_I(\{F_I=0\}\cap S)
\]

has positive \(d\)\-dimensional measure, at least one triple \(I\) satisfies

\[
\mathcal H^d(\{F_I=0\}\cap S)>0.
\]

The restriction \(F_I|_S\) is real analytic.

A nonzero real-analytic function on a connected real-analytic manifold has a zero set of measure zero. Therefore

\[
F_I|_S\equiv0.
\]

Hence the **same original triple \(I\)** forms a unit equilateral triangle throughout \(S\).

Continuity gives

\[
\overline S\cap\mathcal M_n\subseteq\mathcal T_n.
\]

Now take any nonisolated \(X\in\mathcal M_n\). There are distinct optimal configurations converging to \(X\). Because the stratification is finite and its zero-dimensional strata contain only finitely many points, some positive-dimensional stratum \(S\) has \(X\in\overline S\).

Thus \(X\in\mathcal T_n\), proving the first assertion.

The second follows by checking the remaining isolated points. \(\square\)

The analytic zero-set result is established, for example, by Boris Mityagin, *The Zero Set of a Real Analytic Function* (2020). [MathNet.ru](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?jrnid=mzm&option_lang=eng&paperid=12620&wshow=paper&utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**A useful one-dimensional strengthening:** On a connected one-dimensional Nash stratum, infinitely many triangle-bearing optimizers accumulating at an interior point are enough to force one fixed unit triangle throughout the stratum. This follows from the identity theorem for analytic functions of one real variable.

This gives a genuine propagation principle, independent of finite multiplicity. Its limitation is substantial: nothing currently establishes the positive-measure hypothesis on every stratum.

### 3\. Exact geometric obstruction at \(n=8\)

The failure of automatic propagation already occurs among exact global minimizers.

Bezdek and Fodor proved

\[
D_8=\frac1{2\sin(\pi/14)}.
\]

Take a regular heptagon of side length \(1\). Its circumradius is

\[
R=\frac1{2\sin(\pi/7)}.
\]

Orient an edge so its endpoints are

\[
v_0=(m,-\tfrac12),\qquad
v_1=(m,\tfrac12),
\qquad
m=R\cos(\pi/7).
\]

Add an eighth point

\[
p(t)=(t,0),
\qquad
0\le t\le t_*,
\]

where

\[
t_*=m-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}>0.
\]

Numerically, \(t_*\approx0.1722353\).

For the two nearest heptagon vertices,

\[
\|p(t)-v_0\|^2
=\|p(t)-v_1\|^2
=(m-t)^2+\frac14.
\]

Every other heptagon vertex is at least as far from \(p(t)\). Therefore:

- For \(0\le t<t_*\), all distances from \(p(t)\) to the heptagon vertices are strictly greater than \(1\).
- At \(t=t_*\), the distances to both \(v_0\) and \(v_1\) equal \(1\).
- Throughout the interval, \(p(t)\) remains inside the heptagon.

The seven outer vertices already realize diameter \(D_8\). Adding a point inside their convex hull cannot increase that diameter.

Thus **every \(X(t)\) in this path is an exact unrestricted global optimizer**.

For \(t<t_*\), its unit-contact graph is the seven-cycle, so it contains no unit triangle.

At \(t=t_*\),

\[
\|p(t_*)-v_0\|
=\|p(t_*)-v_1\|
=\|v_0-v_1\|=1.
\]

An original \(1\!-\!1\!-\!1\) triangle appears.

The path is nonconstant even modulo congruence: the sum of squared distances between the eighth point and all seven outer vertices equals

\[
7(R^2+t^2).
\]

Hence \(h(8)=\infty\).

**Consequently, triangle-bearing and triangle-free exact global optimizers can belong to the same connected optimal replacement fiber.** The triangle appears only at its boundary, where two new unit contacts become active. This disproves any proposed general rule that merely reaching a triangle-bearing configuration along an optimal arc transfers that triangle backward along the arc.

It is a finite-\(n\) obstruction to a proof method. It does **not** disprove Erdős's eventual conjecture.

The global optimality input is the original Bezdek–Fodor theorem: [Minimal Diameter of Certain Sets in the Plane (1999)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0097316598928898?utm_source=chatgpt.com).

### 4\. Isolated triangle-free points: an exact quadratic countermodel

Semialgebraic stratification does not prevent isolated bad points from coexisting with positive-dimensional good strata.

Consider the compact set

\[
S=\left\{(x,y):
\begin{array}{l}
y(y-1)=0,\\
x(1-y)=0,\\
x-y\ge0,\quad 2y-x\ge0
\end{array}\right\}.
\]

Its exact solution set is

\[
S=\{(0,0)\}\ \cup\ \{(x,1):1\le x\le2\}.
\]

Define the desired-property locus

\[
T=\{(x,y)\in S:y=1\}.
\]

Then \(T\) is closed, contains an entire positive-dimensional stratum, and has infinitely many points. Nevertheless, the isolated point \((0,0)\) fails the property.

All defining equations and inequalities have degree at most two.

This is an **abstract quadratic semialgebraic countermodel**, not a claimed realization by a diameter-minimal planar packing. It proves that quadratic semialgebraicity, positive-dimensional good strata and finiteness of isolated strata cannot by themselves establish the desired all-configurations conclusion.

### 5\. Local replacement fibers and second-order paths

For an exact optimizer \(X\), fix all points except \(x_i\). Its replacement fiber is

\[
\mathcal F_i(X)=
\left\{y\in\mathbb R^2:
1\le\|y-x_j\|\le D_n
\ \text{for every }j\ne i
\right\}.
\]

Every point of \(\mathcal F_i(X)\) produces another **exact global optimizer**, since its diameter is at most \(D_n\), and no valid \(n\)\-point set can have smaller diameter.

This gives an exact, useful way to generate optimal arcs. But the \(n=8\) construction shows that a replacement fiber can contain a two-dimensional triangle-free region as well as triangle-bearing boundary points.

For a twice-differentiable feasible path

\[
x_i(t)=x_i+t v_i+\tfrac12t^2a_i+o(t^2),
\]

write \(r_{ij}=x_i-x_j\), \(v_{ij}=v_i-v_j\) and \(a_{ij}=a_i-a_j\).

At every active unit contact, feasibility requires

\[
r_{ij}\cdot v_{ij}\ge0.
\]

If this first-order expression vanishes, then necessarily

\[
\|v_{ij}\|^2+r_{ij}\cdot a_{ij}\ge0.
\]

At every active diametral pair the corresponding signs reverse:

\[
r_{ij}\cdot v_{ij}\le0,
\]

and, when equality holds,

\[
\|v_{ij}\|^2+r_{ij}\cdot a_{ij}\le0.
\]

These are rigorous necessary conditions. They are **not sufficient** for a realizable arc.

An especially sharp quadratic example is

\[
x-y^2=0,\qquad xy=0.
\]

Its only solution is \((0,0)\). Yet the formal path

\[
x(t)=t^2,\qquad y(t)=t
\]

satisfies both equations through second order. The second equation fails only at order \(t^3\).

Thus an isolated feasible point can admit a nonzero first-order direction and a compatible second-order jet while admitting no nonconstant feasible path.

This does not establish such an obstruction for the special distance inequalities of Erdős #99. It establishes that **a second-order jet argument needs an additional realization theorem** before it can eliminate isolated configurations.

Semialgebraic curve selection supplies an actual analytic arc when a point is already known to be nonisolated; it does not prove nonisolation. [indico.ictp.it](https://indico.ictp.it/event/a02455/session/9/contribution/6/material/0/0.pdf)

### 6\. Exact missing bridge

The analysis separates two genuinely different outstanding obligations.

For **positive-dimensional optimal strata**, one needs a geometric mechanism forcing original unit triangles on a positive-measure subset of each connected analytic stratum, or a different argument directly excluding triangle-free strata. The analytic propagation theorem would then carry the conclusion to every point in those strata and their closures.

For **isolated optimal configurations**, one needs a separate rigidity, stress or global-comparison theorem proving that an isolated triangle-free exact global optimizer cannot exist for sufficiently large \(n\). Positive-dimensional strata elsewhere cannot resolve this case.

A finite semialgebraic stratification makes these categories precise for each fixed \(n\), but supplies no uniform large-\(n\) exclusion. The \(n=8\) family shows that the first obligation is not automatic; the quadratic countermodel shows why the second cannot be discarded.

The contemporary work of Das on stresses and boundary pinning offers relevant geometric constraints, but does not establish either unrestricted obligation. [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/22768362?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

**Research assessment:** The analytic-stratum propagation theorem is proved under its stated hypotheses, and the exact \(n=8\) path rigorously defeats an unconditional arc-transfer principle. The most useful next target is a geometry-specific theorem excluding triangle-free positive-dimensional optimal strata or triangle-free isolated global minimizers. Neither has been established here.

## Proposition: strictly stationary near-optimal n-packings with only O(sqrt n) contacts

For all sufficiently large integers n there exists a planar n-point set `X_n` with minimum separation exactly 1, **triangle-free** original unit-distance graph, `e(X_n)=2*kappa*sqrt(n)+O(1)` with `kappa=sqrt(pi*sqrt(3)/2)`, diameter `D_n <= diam(X_n) < D_n+4`, and a full KKT equilibrium stress whose multipliers are strictly positive **on all active minimum- and maximum-distance constraints**. Here `D_n` is the globally least diameter of n unit-separated planar points. The set is *not asserted* to attain `D_n`.

**Construction.** Define `r=sqrt(sqrt(3)*n/(2*pi))`, even `m=2*ceil(pi*(r+1))`, `R=1/(2*sin(pi/m))`, `s=1+1/n`, and `T=R-1-1/n`. Take the m vertices of a regular even polygon on radius R; its consecutive side length is exactly 1 and there are m/2 diametral antipodal pairs at distance 2R. Put an s-spaced triangular lattice in the disk of radius T, and choose exactly n-m of its points. To establish availability, use triangular Voronoi cells of area `sqrt(3)*s^2/2` and covering radius `s/sqrt(3)`. Their cells show

`N(T) >= 2*pi*(T-s/sqrt(3))^2/(sqrt(3)*s^2)` (for positive inner radius).

Since `r+1<=R<r+3/2` eventually, we have `T>=r-1/n`, and therefore `N(T) >= n-(4*pi/3)*r-O(1)`; meanwhile `m=2*pi*r+O(1)`. The excess `(2*pi/3)*r-O(1)>0` ensures `N(T)>=n-m` eventually. All interior-interior distances exceed 1; all polygon-interior distances are at least `R-T=1+1/n`. Exactly m polygon-side unit contacts remain, so `e(X_n)=m=2*kappa*sqrt(n)+O(1)`. Because all interior points lie at radius T<R, the unique maximum distance value 2R occurs only between antipodal polygon vertices.

**Near-global diameter certificate.** Oler's area/perimeter inequality, with isodiametric bounds, gives `n <= pi*D_n^2/(2*sqrt(3)) + pi*D_n/2 + 1`. At `D=2r-1` the RHS equals `n+pi*r*(1-2/sqrt(3))+O(1)<n` eventually, hence `D_n>2r-1`. Also `2R<2r+3`; therefore `0<=2R-D_n<4`. This proves **additive** near-optimality only.

**Exact KKT check.** Minimize squared-diameter variable `t` subject to every `1-|x_i-x_j|^2<=0` and `|x_i-x_j|^2-t<=0`. Set `mu=2/m>0` on each of the m/2 diametral antipodal pairs, and `lambda=mu/(1-cos(2*pi/m))>0` on each of the m sides. Every interior vertex is incident to no active pair. At polygon vertex v, the sum of contributions to the positional Lagrangian gradient is

`4*mu*v - 4*lambda*(1-cos(2*pi/m))*v = 0`.

The scalar derivative is `1-(m/2)*mu=0`. Choosing velocity `dot(v)=v` at each polygon vertex, fixing interior points, and `dot(t)=3t` strictly relaxes all active constraints: side squared-distances increase at rate 2, and diametral squared-distance constraints decrease at rate `2t-3t=-t`. Thus MFCQ holds as well. The claim of *strictly positive multipliers on every active constraint* is verified, subject to the eventual-n Voronoi count above.

**Proposition (finite geometric equilibrium, conditional on positive stress).** Let `X` be a finite set of distinct points of mutual distance at least 1 and diameter `D>1`. Suppose there are nonnegative equilibrium multipliers on the unit-contact edges and diametral edges, positive precisely on some support, obeying

`sum_{j, |xi-xj|=1} lambda_ij (xi-xj) = sum_{j, |xi-xj|=D} mu_ij (xi-xj)`

at every vertex, with `lambda,mu >=0`. **If the positive diametral edges are at least two distinct edges and ALL have one common endpoint `a`, then X contains an ORIGINAL unit equilateral triple.** Other geometrically diametral pairs are permitted with zero multiplier. No global-minimality premise is needed after assuming this equilibrium.

**Proof, including support/maximum principle detail.** Write the positive diameter edges `a b_1,...,a b_k` with `k>=2`, and `P={a,b_1,...,b_k}`. Since all `|a-b_i|=D` and `|b_i-b_j|<=D`, the direction angles `b_i-a` lie in a sector of angular width at most 60 degrees. (Relative to any one direction, all lie within +/-60 degrees; any directions occurring on opposite sides differ by at most 60 degrees because their chord is at most D.) Let `b_-` and `b_+` be the distinct extreme rays and `K=conv(P)`; K is contained in the closed sector bounded by the rays `a b_-` and `a b_+`.

Let `C+` denote the positive unit-contact graph. Each connected component containing at least one positive-contact edge meets P: otherwise every vertex satisfies the harmonic equation `xi=(sum lambda_ij xj)/(sum lambda_ij)`; a nonconstant real coordinate attains an interior maximum, propagating equality to all neighboring sites, and a connected nontrivial component would collapse to one point. The same discrete maximum principle with Dirichlet boundary P shows **every vertex incident to a positive contact belongs to K**. This is applied component by component; vertices with no positive support do not enter the argument. Both `b_-` and `b_+` have positive unit-contact degree because their positive diametral forces are nonzero.

Choose an inward unit normal `w_-` to the supporting line `a b_-`, so `w_- . z >= w_- . a = w_- . b_- =0` for all supported contact vertices z. At `b_-`, the only positive diameter edge is `a b_-`, whose force is parallel to the boundary line. Dotting the equilibrium with `w_-` yields `sum_{j in C+(b_-)} lambda (w_- . xj)=0`. Every summand is nonnegative, so **every positive contact neighbor of b_- lies on the closed segment [a,b_-]**. The unique possible neighbor at distance one is `b_- - (b_--a)/D`.

Continue toward a along this boundary. At a positive-contact neighbor `v` on [a,b_-], other than a and b_-, v carries no positive diameter edge (all other diameter leaves are at distance D from a on different rays). The boundary-normal component of its harmonic equation forces ALL its positive contact neighbors onto [a,b_-]. Its known neighbor one unit farther from a exerts a nonzero longitudinal force, so its equilibrium requires a positive contact neighbor one unit closer to a. There is exactly one such position along the segment. Induction either reaches a through unit-length steps or would require a contact outside the segment; the latter contradicts harmonic equilibrium. Thus **D is a positive integer**, and in particular the ORIGINAL point `u_- = a+(b_--a)/D` belongs to X. Repeating on the other extreme boundary gives ORIGINAL `u_+=a+(b_+-a)/D`. They are distinct unit-distance points from a, and

`|u_- - u_+|=|b_- - b_+|/D <=1`.

Unit separation makes this equality. Hence `a,u_-,u_+` form an exact original equilateral triangle of side one. QED.

**Why the assumptions matter:** the global n=5 unit regular pentagon has a positive mixed block with FIVE positive diameter edges, but its diameter-positive graph is a 5-cycle, not a star. The n=4 unit square has two positive disjoint crossing diameter edges, also not a star. Thus this proposition cannot directly exclude arbitrary mixed positive blocks with three or more diameter edges whose supports include several endpoints, nor prove the original all-global assertion. ROOT checked the elementary harmonic, boundary-force, unit-chain and chord arguments; no independent third-party referee for the star extension yet.

## 2. Hypatia's partition-cut obstruction — ROOT verified signs

Let an exact global optimizer `X=A union B` have `D>1`, and suppose **all geometrically active diameter pairs cross this partition**. Orient crossing vectors consistently as `xi-xj`, `i in A`, `j in B`. Let `M` be the finite set of active diameter vectors and `C` the crossing original unit-contact vectors. Then necessarily

`conv(M) intersect cone(C) != empty`, with `cone(empty)={0}`.

If the sets were disjoint, the compact convex hull and closed finitely-generated cone admit strict separating `v` with `m.v<0` for all m in M and `c.v>=0` for every c in C. Translate the A-points by `+t v`. Internal pairs are unchanged; crossing unit distances satisfy `|c+t v|^2=1+2t(c.v)+t^2|v|^2>=1`, while every currently active diameter pair strictly decreases for small positive t. Finite slack protects every nonactive pair, contradicting exact global optimality. This is an exact, same-n descent, not merely KKT stationarity. It does not force a positive density of unit contacts. # Erdős #99 — ROOT Oler–Reuleaux exclusion of an equilateral diameter triple (2026-10-31)

**Original conjecture remains OPEN:** `exists N for all n>=N for all exact unrestricted global diameter minimizers X of n planar unit-separated original sites: X contains an ORIGINAL equilateral triangle of side EXACTLY 1`. This record instead proves a useful theorem about equilateral triangles of side **the full diameter** `D_n`. No historical originality claim.

## Proposition (ROOT derivation from published Oler inequality)

For every `n>=1000` and **every** exact global diameter minimizer `X` of `n` pairwise unit-separated planar sites, **no three original points have all three mutual distances equal to `D_n`**. Thus the complete geometric diameter graph has **no triangle** for every `n>=1000`.

### Proof

Set `D=D_n`, and suppose a,b,c in X form an equilateral triangle of side D. Every original point lies within distance D of each of a,b,c by the diameter definition, so the convex hull `K=conv(X)` lies inside the width-D Reuleaux triangle `R = B_D(a) intersect B_D(b) intersect B_D(c)`. Its area and perimeter are exactly

`A(R) = (pi - sqrt(3))*D^2/2`, `P(R)=pi*D`.

Area and perimeter are monotone under inclusion of planar convex bodies. Oler's finite unit-separated packing inequality (1961) therefore gives

`n <= 2 A(K)/sqrt(3) + P(K)/2 + 1 <= alpha D^2 + (pi/2) D + 1`,

where `alpha=pi/sqrt(3)-1`.

The unit triangular lattice has fundamental area `sqrt(3)/2`; its expected count in a uniformly translated **open** disk of diameter L is `beta L^2`, where `beta=pi/(2sqrt(3))`. Take `L=sqrt((n+1)/beta)`. Some translate contains at least `n+1` lattice points in that disk (mean count `n+1`, and the count is integer); selecting any n yields a unit-separated set of diameter at most L. Consequently `D_n <= sqrt((n+1)/beta)`. Combining,

`n <= (alpha/beta)*(n+1) + (pi/2)*sqrt((n+1)/beta) + 1`,

with `alpha/beta=2-2sqrt(3)/pi <9/10`, `beta>9/10`, and `pi/2<8/5`. The bounds follow, for example, from `3.14<pi<22/7` and `1.73<sqrt(3)<1.74`.

For `n>=1000`, `sqrt((n+1)/beta) < sqrt((n+1)/(9/10)) <= (n+1)/30` (because `(9/10)*(n+1)>=900`). Thus

`n < (9/10)*(n+1) + (8/5)*(n+1)/30 + 1 = (143/150)*(n+1)+1`,

which implies `7n < 293`, impossible for n>=1000. QED.

The threshold 1000 is deliberately coarse, avoiding any reliance on numerical optimization or decimal evidence. As an elementary check, the exact inequality already contradicts n=300, but the proof above needs only safe rational comparisons. The only non-elementary input is Oler's published theorem and its stated finite-packing hypotheses.

## Direct anchored homothety lemma

Let `X` be a finite unit-separated configuration, diameter `D`, and full unit-contact graph `G`. Suppose a nonempty subset `S` contains **no original diameter endpoints**, and **every** unit contact crossing from `S` to `X\S` meets one common external anchor `a` (the crossing set may be empty). Hold `X\S` fixed and set `x(t)=a+(1+t)(x-a)` for `x` in `S`. Every unit contact within `S` or crossing to `a` grows strictly. Every other crossing distance is initially strictly greater than one, and all pairs incident with `S` have distances strictly less than `D`, so all these inequalities remain admissible for sufficiently small positive `t`. An original diameter pair outside `S` stays fixed and keeps the diameter exactly `D`; no new unit contacts arise. Thus

`e(X(t))=e(X)-e(X[S])-e(S,X\S)`.

**A contact must actually be present** among these two removed sets to force strict decrease of contact count. A subset with no internal or crossing contact gives no contradiction. Because the contact graph only loses edges, any pre-existing triangle-free property is preserved.

## A triangle-free nearhex family with diverging bulk area defect but diameter gap below 3

For each integer `n>=16` let `theta=pi/3+n^(-1/2) in (pi/3,pi/2)`, `u=(1,0)`, `v=(cos(theta),sin(theta))`, and `L=Z u+Z v`. Let `P_n` consist of the `n` lattice sites nearest the origin; break ties arbitrarily. Write `a=sqrt(3)/2`, `s=sin(theta)`, and `D_n` for the **unrestricted** smallest diameter of any planar `n`-point set with separation `>=1`.

As the basis is a Gauss-reduced equal-length rhombic basis with `theta in (pi/3,pi/2)`, nonzero lattice distances are `>=1`, and equality occurs only for `+/-u,+/-v`. Thus `P_n` has a bipartite original unit-contact graph and **no original exact unit equilateral triangle**.

The full-lattice Voronoi cell has six positive facets corresponding to `+/-u,+/-v,+/-(u-v)`, area `s` and covering radius `rho=1/(2cos(theta/2))`. If `r_n=max_{x in P_n}|x|`, tiling the disk by full-lattice Voronoi cells gives

`r_n <= sqrt(n*s/pi)+rho`, hence `diam(P_n) <= 2sqrt(n*s/pi)+1/cos(theta/2)`.

Only `O(r_n)=O(sqrt(n))` selected lattice sites lie in a boundary strip of fixed width `2`; each selected site at `|x|<=r_n-2` has all six mentioned original neighbors within `P_n`, and its ORIGINAL full Voronoi cell equals that of the infinite lattice. It follows that the bulk total of the six-facet ORIGINAL full-cell triangular area excess is

`E_bulk(P_n) = (n-O(sqrt(n)))*(sin(theta)-a) = (1/2)*sqrt(n)+O(1)`, 

where the final asymptotic follows from `sin(pi/3+delta)-a=delta/2+O(delta^2)`, `delta=1/sqrt(n)`. In particular, `E_bulk -> infinity` with no exact original unit triangle.

Classical Oler's inequality plus isodiametric and perimeter bounds imply `n<=pi*D_n^2/(2sqrt(3))+pi*D_n/2+1` and therefore

`D_n >= sqrt((2sqrt(3)/pi)*(n-1)+3/4)-sqrt(3)/2`.

Since the sine function is concave on this angle interval, `sin(theta)-a <=1/(2sqrt(n))`, and `sqrt(sin(theta))-sqrt(a) <= (sin(theta)-a)/(2sqrt(a))`. Consequently, with `C=sqrt(2sqrt(3)/pi)`,

`0 <= diam(P_n)-D_n <= 1/cos(theta/2) + sqrt(3)/2 + C*(sqrt(n)-sqrt(n-1)) + 1/(2sqrt(pi*a))`.

Even using the deliberately weaker last term `1/sqrt(pi*a)`, the RHS is a decreasing function of `n>=16` and at `n=16` is `2.8604773460052213 < 3`. Thus the original proposed bound `0<=diam(P_n)-D_n<3` holds provided the lattice counting and Voronoi facts above are verified; it **does not** assert equality with the global optimum.

**Precise no-go.** There is no universal positive `c` for which `diam(P)-D_n >= c*E_bulk(P)` holds for *all* triangle-free unit-separated nearhex `n`-point sets if `E_bulk` is defined as the above total ORIGINAL full Voronoi-cell excess at all six-facet bulk sites: the left side remains below `3`, whereas `E_bulk(P_n)->infinity`.
